Chebyshev, Elliptic and Bessel Filters, and Window-Method FIR Design (L10)

Why this matters in the exam: L10 has never been tested. Sample Test 1 covered only L02–L04, so filter design is a strong candidate for the final. Tutorial 9 is the only practice set, and its non-Butterworth questions show the likely patterns: find and for a Chebyshev filter (T9 Q7), fill in a sample to make linear phase and prove it (T9 Q8), and design a short windowed FIR filter by hand (T9 Q9). Sample Test 1 gave 4–7 marks per question (5, 4, 4, 7 out of 20), so expect parts of about that size. Each one is a short, mechanical calculation if you know the playbook. Pack D11 covers the bilinear transform and Butterworth design. This pack assumes you can pre-warp: .

1.5 The four families compared (L10 slides 29–32)

Butterworth Chebyshev I Chebyshev II Elliptic (Cauer) Bessel
Passband maximally flat, monotonic equiripple monotonic equiripple smooth, droops
Stopband monotonic monotonic equiripple equiripple monotonic, slow
Poles / zeros all-pole, on a circle of radius all-pole, on an ellipse poles and zeros (zeros on axis) poles and zeros (zeros on axis) all-pole,
Order for a given spec medium lower lower (same as I) lowest highest
Phase fairly smooth more nonlinear more nonlinear most nonlinear linear in passband (lost after bilinear mapping)
Course design formulas , (D11) , , poles , none (qualitative only) none (qualitative only)

1.6 Linear-phase FIR filters (L10 slides 33–36, L09 slides 9–10)

A length- FIR filter has linear phase if is

  • symmetric: , or
  • antisymmetric: . If is odd, this forces the middle sample .

The centre of symmetry is . Factor out and the rest is real:

The group delay is samples. When changes sign, the phase jumps by . It is still called linear (see T9 Q8).

The four types below are the standard textbook naming. L10 does not use the labels, but it gives both symmetries, and the zero rules follow directly from them. Use them to answer “can this filter be a highpass?”.

Type Symmetry built from Forced zeros Cannot be
I symmetric odd none (any response OK)
II symmetric even () highpass, bandstop
III antisymmetric odd and lowpass, highpass, bandstop
IV antisymmetric even () lowpass, bandstop

All types have the same extra rule. Real coefficients and symmetry mean that if is a zero, so are , and . Zeros come in reciprocal groups (four, two on the unit circle or real axis, or one at ).

1.7 Window design (L10 slides 38–41)

The ideal lowpass filter with cutoff has the inverse DTFT (T9 Q1)

(Slide 38 prints the inverse DTFT with . It should be .)

Sinc convention. The course uses . MATLAB and numpy use . So the course’s is (wc/pi)*np.sinc(wc*n/pi) in Python. T9 Q1 points this out.

Why the ideal filter cannot be built (T9 Q1): for , so it is non-causal. It is also infinitely long.

The fix (slide 38): shift by , then truncate with a window that is symmetric about :

Including a general , , with value at .

Multiplying by in time convolves with in frequency (slide 39). The mainlobe of smears the transition. The sidelobes cause passband and stopband ripple.

Windows exactly as L10 slide 41 defines them (, zero elsewhere):

Window values values
Rectangular 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 all 1
Bartlett 0, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0 0, 0.3333, 0.6667, 1, …
Hanning 0, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0 0, 0.25, 0.75, 1, …
Hamming 0.08, 0.54, 1, 0.54, 0.08 0.08, 0.31, 0.77, 1, …
Blackman 0, 0.34, 1, 0.34, 0 0, 0.13, 0.63, 1, …

Properties (computed with scipy for and these exact definitions; the course shows them only as plots on slides 42–44):

Window Mainlobe width Peak sidelobe of Min. stopband attenuation of the filter
Rectangular −13 dB −21 dB
Bartlett −26 dB −26 dB
Hanning −31 dB −44 dB
Hamming −42 dB −53 dB
Blackman −58 dB −75 dB

The trade-off: a taper gives lower sidelobes but a wider mainlobe, which means a wider transition band.

  • Trap: the course windows use in the denominator, so Bartlett, Hanning and Blackman are zero at both ends. For , Hanning and Bartlett give the same window. These match scipy’s windows.hann(M), hamming(M), blackman(M) and bartlett(M), and MATLAB’s hann, not MATLAB’s hanning, which drops the zero end points.
  • Trap: scipy.signal.firwin scales the filter to unit DC gain by default. Pass scale=False to match the course. The cutoff is given as .

This starts at Example 3 (, ). Switch between rectangular and Hamming and compare and with the table there. Then raise to about 31 and watch Hamming keep a flat passband with much lower sidelobes.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using in the Chebyshev formula. The arguments are greater than 1. Use .
  • Forgetting to pre-warp before forming for a digital design. For T9 Q7 the unwarped ratio is exactly 2. The warped ratio is 2.0515.
  • Getting for Type II from the stopband. In the course, always comes from .
  • Rounding to the nearest integer instead of up. 5.09 → 6.
  • Even- Chebyshev I with . For even the DC gain is , not 1.
  • Antisymmetric, odd , middle sample not zero. forces it to be 0 (T9 Q8).
  • Window with instead of in the cosine, or MATLAB’s hanning. The course Hanning with is . Also, forgetting to shift: you must use , not .
  • Sinc confusion. The course’s is np.sinc(n/6)/6 in numpy. Writing np.sinc(np.pi*n/6) is wrong by a factor of in the argument.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

CHEBYSHEV (I and II, same eps and N)          [L10 s24, s27]
  dp = 10^(-Rp/20), ds = 10^(-As/20)
  eps = sqrt(1/dp^2 - 1)          (1 dB -> 0.5088, 0.5 dB -> 0.3493)
  N = acosh( sqrt(1-ds^2)/(eps*ds) ) / acosh(Ws/Wp)   ROUND UP
      acosh x = ln(x + sqrt(x^2-1)); slides print "cos^-1"
  Digital: Wi = 2 tan(wi/2) (T=1) BEFORE taking Ws/Wp
  Type I : equiripple passband, |H(0)|=1 (N odd) or dp (N even), all-pole
  Type II: equiripple stopband, zeros at W = Ws/cos((2k+1)pi/2N)
CHEB I POLES  beta = ((sqrt(1+eps^2)+1)/eps)^(1/N)
  r1 = Wp(beta^2+1)/(2beta) [jW axis], r2 = Wp(beta^2-1)/(2beta) [sigma]
  phi_k = 90 + (2k+1)180/(2N) deg ; p_k = r2 cos phi_k + j r1 sin phi_k
  K = prod(-p_k) (N odd), /sqrt(1+eps^2) (N even)
FAMILIES  order: Elliptic < Cheb I = Cheb II < Butter < Bessel
          phase: Bessel best ... Elliptic worst
LINEAR PHASE FIR  alpha=(M-1)/2, group delay = alpha
  sym: H = e^{-j alpha w} A(w)   antisym: H = e^{-j(alpha w - pi/2)} A(w)
  I sym/odd: any | II sym/even: zero z=-1 (no HP)
  III anti/odd: h(alpha)=0, zeros z=+-1 (BP only) | IV anti/even: zero z=1 (no LP)
  Fill: compare ends -> sym or anti; mirror about alpha
WINDOW METHOD  hd(n) = sin(wc n)/(pi n), hd(0)=wc/pi
  course sinc x = sin x / x  -> numpy: (wc/pi)*np.sinc(wc*n/pi)
  h(n) = hd(n - alpha) w(n),  n = 0..M-1
  Rect 1 | Bartlett 1-2|n-alpha|/(M-1) | Hanning 0.5(1-cos(2pi n/(M-1)))
  Hamming 0.54-0.46cos(2pi n/(M-1)) | Blackman 0.42-0.5cos(.)+0.08cos(2.)
  M=5: Hanning=Bartlett={0,.5,1,.5,0}; Hamming={.08,.54,1,.54,.08}
  stopband: rect -21, Bart -26, Hanning -44, Hamm -53, Black -75 dB
  A(w) = h(alpha) + 2 sum h(n) cos((alpha-n)w)  -> check at 0, wc, pi
FREQ TRANSFORMS (analogue)  HP: s -> Wp Wp'/s
  BP: s -> Wp (s^2+Wl Wu)/(s(Wu-Wl)), centre sqrt(Wl Wu), order doubles
  Digital HP: z^-1 -> -(z^-1+a)/(1+a z^-1), a = -cos((wp+wp')/2)/cos((wp-wp')/2)
  Check: new edge has the same gain as the prototype edge
